title: Francis King and how Honolulu has changed
summary: He names the sextet's Korean trumpeter and contrasts the old Honolulu with today's tall buildings and tourism.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: You said also that while you were in Honolulu, playing with the Symphony, you had a Jazz sextet, the Red Callender Sextet...
...and you mentioned the nationality of the various musicians, but could you give me their names?

Yes. The trumpet player was Francis King. Francis King, the trumpet player, was of Korean extraction. The funny thing about that, during the time I lived in Honolulu, nobody ever bothered to lock their door even. Like, the mailman used to just bring your packages or whatever, and leave it on the doorstep -- nobody ever touched it. Well, since that time, Francis King has become a millionaire selling burglar alarms. [LAUGHS] See how things change?
He doesn't play trumpet any more.
Oh, he doesn't have to. When I first went to the islands, the tallest building was the Mawana(?) Hotel, which was next door to the Royal Hawaiian. Now

there's a Sheraton Hotel. I think that's about 33 stories. Trummy Young plays on the top floor, incidentally, still. But the whole island now looks like downtown New York rather than Los Angeles. And there's smog there even. Can you picture that? On a beautiful island, there's so many cars and so many tall buildings, you can't even see the ocean. I lived in Waikiki in a little one-room apartment on Lialokalani, and I could see the ocean from my window. Now that street has been discontinued. They've bypassed it, and it's now part of Don Ho Lane or Don Ho Village. So things do change. Honolulu now... Well, I wouldn't want to live there now anyhow, because it's really a tourist trap.
